opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that architecture innovation has, for now, run ahead of what our data can actually support.

Over the last couple of years, a lot of the energy in robot learning went into the model side: how to tokenize actions, whether to use diffusion or flow matching for the action head, how to connect a vision-language backbone to a low-level policy, how to handle different control frequencies. That work mattered, and it got us to a point where the architectures are reasonably mature. If you hand a good team a large, clean, well-structured dataset today, they can build a model that absorbs it pretty well.

The problem is that we don't have that dataset. In language, the internet gave everyone a huge shared corpus almost for free, so the field could compete on architecture and scaling recipes. In robotics, data is scarce, expensive, and messy. It comes from different embodiments, different sensors, different camera placements, different action spaces, and often wildly different quality levels. So when we design the system architecture-first and then try to pour data into it, a lot of that data either doesn't fit or ends up as noise.

"Data-native" means flipping the order. You start by asking: what data can we realistically get at scale, from teleoperation, from human videos, from simulation, from deployed robots in the field? What structure does that data naturally have? Then you design the representation, the training objectives, and even the hardware and collection pipeline around it. The model becomes something that grows out of the data, rather than a container the data has to be forced into.

There's a practical side too. When we looked at where our improvements actually came from, the big jumps usually came from changing data: better coverage of failure and recovery, more diverse scenes, cleaner action labels, better mixing ratios, rather than another architectural tweak. Once you see that pattern clearly, it would be strange not to reorganize around it.

And longer term, I think it's the only path to a real foundation model for robots. A foundation model is only as general as the distribution it has seen. If we want robots that work in homes, factories, and stores, the bottleneck is building a data engine that keeps expanding that distribution, where deployment generates data, data improves the model, and the better model enables wider deployment. Designing around that loop is what I mean by data-native, and I believe that's where the next order-of-magnitude progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response mentions different embodiments and broader deployment settings, but does not identify generalization across robot body morphologies as a goal.

r002.rationale: The response says robot data is scarce and calls for expanding its scale and distribution, but does not state that task generalization requires especially large amounts of data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we've spent the past two years squeezing most of what there is to squeeze out of architecture.

When we started, the big questions were structural. Do you use a VLM backbone or train from scratch? Diffusion head or autoregressive tokens? How do you fuse proprioception with vision? Those were real questions, and the answers mattered. But at this point the community has mostly converged. If you look at the leading robot foundation models today, the architectures are maybe ten percent different from each other. You swap one for another and the downstream behavior barely changes. That's a signal. When the architecture stops being the bottleneck, something else is.

And what's left is data. Not just more data, but the question of what data we actually need, and in what mix. Right now most teams, including us at some stage, were doing what I'd call architecture-native design: you fix the model, then you go find whatever data fits it. Teleoperation episodes in a particular format, a particular camera setup, because that's what the model expects. The model dictates the data.

Data-native flips that. You start from the question: what does the world of robot experience actually look like? There's a tiny amount of high-quality on-robot teleoperation, a lot more cross-embodiment data from other labs with different arms and different cameras, an enormous amount of human egocentric video, simulation data that's cheap but imperfect, and then the model's own rollouts once it's deployed. Each of those has a different noise profile, a different action space, a different degree of grounding. A data-native design asks: how do I build a model and a training recipe whose shape comes from that distribution, rather than forcing the distribution into the shape of a model?

Concretely that changes a lot. Your tokenization has to handle heterogeneous action spaces instead of assuming one. Your loss has to be aware that a human video gives you intention but not actuator commands, so you don't pretend it does. Your curriculum has to decide when to lean on cheap simulation and when to trust the expensive real episodes. Even your evaluation changes, because you stop asking "did it fit the benchmark" and start asking "did the model extract what this data source was actually able to teach it."

The reason I call it the biggest next step rather than just an engineering improvement is that it's the thing that lets the flywheel actually turn. In language, scaling worked because the data was already there, so architecture was the lever. In robotics the data isn't there yet, so the lever is designing the system around how data gets generated and consumed. Once you do that, every deployed robot becomes a data source, every new embodiment becomes an input rather than a migration project, and scaling starts to look like it did for language. Until then we're just building nicer and nicer models for a dataset that doesn't exist.

r001.rationale: It describes training on cross-embodiment data and says each new embodiment should become an input rather than a migration project, communicating support across robot morphologies.

r002.rationale: It discusses robotics data scarcity and the need to design around data sources, but does not state that task generalization requires especially large amounts of data.

astra-6.text:
Because it changes where the capability comes from. In an architecture-native approach, we try to build more of our assumptions about robotics into the model itself. In a data-native approach, the focus shifts toward learning from diverse experience—and building a system that can keep improving as that experience grows.

That matters for robots because the real world is so varied. You can design around a particular task or environment, but you can’t anticipate every object, every contact, or every way an action might fail. We want the model to learn transferable behavior from those experiences, rather than requiring a new design for each situation.

The challenge, then, isn’t simply collecting more data. It’s making data from different tasks and robots useful together, preserving the information that matters for action, and feeding failures back into learning. Architecture still matters, but its role is to support that process. That’s why I see this as the next big step: moving toward a model whose capabilities can grow with its experience.

r001.rationale: It mentions learning from different robots, but does not clearly identify generalization across robot body morphologies as a goal.

r002.rationale: It discusses diverse experience and says the challenge is not simply collecting more data; it does not state that task generalization requires especially large amounts of data.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as the biggest next step because it changes where we expect generalization to come from. In an architecture-native approach, we put a lot of our assumptions into the model: how it represents the world, how it plans, and how it produces actions. That can work well, but each new task or robot may require another design decision.

A data-native approach starts with a different question: what experience does the model need, and how do we collect and represent that experience so it can learn across tasks and embodiments? Architecture still matters, but it supports learning from data instead of carrying so much of the solution itself.

For robotics, that’s particularly challenging because experience is physical. Different robots have different bodies, sensors, and action spaces, and collecting interactions takes time. So the next step isn’t simply making the model bigger. It’s building a data pipeline where successes, failures, and new environments can consistently improve the model. That creates a path toward broader capabilities without having to redesign the system for every new task.

r001.rationale: The response says data-native learning should generalize across embodiments and notes that robots have different bodies, communicating generalization across robot morphologies as a goal.

r002.rationale: It discusses collecting physical experience and improving the model from data, but does not state that task generalization requires especially large amounts of data.
